doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Woody Herman, Chubby Jackson and Europe
title: Writing his book and drug use in the Woody Herman band
summary: Gibbs is writing a memoir with Cary Ginell; now he can discuss the heroin and drinking in the Four Brothers band and what happened to Getz, Sims, Cohn and Chaloff.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: I read a humorous anecdote about you and Buddy Rich.
About the leaving me in the desert?
That’s been in a million — I’m doing a book right now.

And the first chapter has been sent in. I gave them the television chapter because they know I’m a jazz musician, there’ll be a lot about jazz musicians, and I gave him the Steve Allen and Regis Philbins and Don Rickles and the Milton Berles, and all the things I had something to do with my television experience. So they liked it. Now when I get back, I’m writing with a gentleman called Cary Ginell, who produced an NPR show, a Nancy Wilson thing, for my 75th birthday. And he’s editing the thing with me. So we just did a chapter, which they wanted, on the Woody Herman Four Brothers band. And I could talk about things now that I couldn’t ten years ago. Because unfortunately there was a lot of dope in that band. A lot of junkies. Sick guys. Which I wouldn’t talk about and mention
names. But I can talk about it now. Because I look for humor in everything. Things that weren’t funny then, I can look now and they were funny but tragic at the same time.
Did some of the fellas that were into that suffer later on? Even if they got over it?

They — Stan Getz, Zoot Sims, Al Cohn and Serge Chaloff all died I think from cirrhosis of the liver. Even though they quit. Even when they quit though, they were all drinking. Stan Getz would drink a fifth of liquor and it wouldn’t bother him like it would the guy who never made that. But they were all straight later on. But I think what happened is it affected them. It stays in your system I suppose. Thank God I never did that, and let me tell you one of the reasons. Two things. I like to laugh. And all the junkies I’ve seen they don’t even laugh, they’re just like falling asleep. And the second reason, which is the most important reason, is I am afraid of a needle. When I go to the doctor for a shot in my fanny of penicillin, he’s got to catch me before I get — then I’ll take that thing if I get a cold. Needles don’t do anything for me. Not my favorite thing in the world.
